final_proof:
**Conventions.** A line through the origin making angle $\alpha$ with the $x$-axis is the set $L_\alpha=\{t(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha): t\in\mathbb R\}$. Since $L_\alpha=L_{\alpha+\pi}$, the angle is determined modulo $\pi$; we take $\theta,\phi\in[0,\pi)$ (so "$\theta=\pi/2$" means that $M$ is the $y$-axis, i.e. $\cos\theta=0$). Thus $M=L_\theta$, $N=L_\phi$. Write $u=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, $v=(\cos\phi,\sin\phi)$.

**Step 0: the projection is well defined, and the case split is exhaustive.** Since $\theta,\phi\in[0,\pi)$ and $M\neq N$, we have $\theta\neq\phi$, so $0<|\theta-\phi|<\pi$ and hence $\sin(\phi-\theta)\neq 0$. The line through $P$ parallel to $N$ is $N_P=\{P+sv : s\in\mathbb R\}$ (the unique line through $P$ with direction $v$; if $P\in N$ it is $N$ itself). A point of $M\cap N_P$ corresponds to a solution $(t,s)$ of $tu - sv = P$, a $2\times2$ linear system with determinant
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -\cos\phi\\ \sin\theta & -\sin\phi\end{pmatrix} = -\cos\theta\sin\phi+\sin\theta\cos\phi=-\sin(\phi-\theta)\neq 0,$$
so there is exactly one solution, and $M\cap N_P$ is a single point. Hence $\mathrm{pr}_{M,N}(P)$ is well defined, and to identify it, it suffices to exhibit a point lying on both $M$ and $N_P$.

Because $\theta\ne\phi$ in $[0,\pi)$, the conditions $\theta=\pi/2$ and $\phi=\pi/2$ cannot both hold, so the three cases below are mutually exclusive and cover all possibilities. In the "otherwise" case $\cos\theta\neq0\neq\cos\phi$, so $\tan\theta,\tan\phi$ are defined, and $\tan\phi-\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\phi\cos\theta-\cos\phi\sin\theta}{\cos\theta\cos\phi}=\dfrac{\sin(\phi-\theta)}{\cos\theta\cos\phi}\neq0$, so all denominators in the formula are nonzero.

**Useful descriptions.** If $\cos\alpha\ne0$, then $L_\alpha=\{(X,Y): Y=X\tan\alpha\}$: indeed $t(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ satisfies $Y=t\sin\alpha=(t\cos\alpha)\tan\alpha=X\tan\alpha$, and conversely $(X,X\tan\alpha)=t(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ with $t=X/\cos\alpha$. Similarly, if $\cos\phi\neq 0$ then $N_P=\{(X,Y): Y-y=(X-x)\tan\phi\}$ (same argument applied to $(X-x,Y-y)=sv$). If $\cos\alpha=0$ (i.e. $\alpha=\pi/2$), then $L_\alpha=\{(0,Y):Y\in\mathbb R\}$, and $N_P=\{(x,Y):Y\in\mathbb R\}$ when $\phi=\pi/2$.

**Case 1: $\theta=\pi/2$.** Then $\phi\neq\pi/2$, $M$ is the $y$-axis $\{(0,Y)\}$ and $N_P=\{(X,Y):Y-y=(X-x)\tan\phi\}$. The point $Q=(0,\,y-x\tan\phi)$ lies on $M$ (first coordinate $0$) and on $N_P$, since $(y-x\tan\phi)-y=(0-x)\tan\phi$. By Step 0, $\mathrm{pr}_{M,N}(P)=(0,\,y-x\tan\phi)$.

**Case 2: $\phi=\pi/2$.** Then $\theta\ne\pi/2$, $M=\{(X,Y):Y=X\tan\theta\}$ and $N_P$ is the vertical line $\{(x,Y)\}$. The point $Q=(x,\,x\tan\theta)$ lies on both. By Step 0, $\mathrm{pr}_{M,N}(P)=(x,\,x\tan\theta)$.

**Case 3 (otherwise): $\theta\neq\pi/2\neq\phi$.** Then $M=\{Y=X\tan\theta\}$ and $N_P=\{Y-y=(X-x)\tan\phi\}$, and $D:=\tan\phi-\tan\theta\ne0$. Suppose $(X,Y)\in M\cap N_P$. Substituting $Y=X\tan\theta$ into the second equation gives $X\tan\theta-y=X\tan\phi-x\tan\phi$, i.e. $X(\tan\phi-\tan\theta)=x\tan\phi-y$, so
$$X=\frac{x\tan\phi}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}-\frac{y}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}.$$
Then
$$Y=X\tan\theta=\frac{\tan\theta\,(x\tan\phi-y)}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}=\frac{\tan\theta\,(y-x\tan\phi)}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}=\frac{y\tan\theta}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}-\frac{x\tan\theta\tan\phi}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}.$$
Conversely, this $(X,Y)$ satisfies $Y=X\tan\theta$ by construction and $X\tan\theta - y = X\tan\phi - x\tan\phi$ by the choice of $X$ (reverse the algebra, dividing was by $D\neq0$), i.e. $Y-y=(X-x)\tan\phi$; so it lies on $M\cap N_P$. By Step 0,
$$\mathrm{pr}_{M,N}(P)=\left(\frac{x\tan\phi}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}-\frac{y}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta},\ \frac{y\tan\theta}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}-\frac{x\tan\theta\tan\phi}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}\right).$$

Combining the three cases gives exactly the stated formula. $\blacksquare$
